title: ML System Design
description: Design production ML systems covering feature stores, training pipelines, model serving, A/B testing, vector databases, and HNSW indexing.

segments.text: Building a machine learning model is maybe ten percent of the work. The other ninety percent is the system around it: data pipelines, feature stores, model serving, and monitoring. Let's design that system.

A feature store is a centralized repository for ML features. It solves feature reuse across teams, ensures training-serving consistency, and handles both batch features and real-time features from streaming sources.

The training pipeline ingests data, computes features, trains the model, validates it against holdout data, and registers it in a model registry. Each step is versioned. Reproducibility is non-negotiable.
Model serving has two patterns. Online serving returns predictions in milliseconds for real-time requests. Batch serving pre-computes predictions for millions of items offline. Many systems use both.
Here is a challenge for you.
segments.thought_prompt: You deploy a new recommendation model. How do you know if it is actually better than the old one in production?

segments.text: A/B testing. Route a percentage of users to the new model and compare metrics against the control group running the old model. Measure click-through rate, conversion, or revenue. Statistical significance tells you which model wins.

Vector databases store high-dimensional embeddings and find similar items fast. Instead of exact search across millions of vectors, they use approximate nearest neighbor algorithms. The trade-off: speed for a small accuracy loss.

HNSW, Hierarchical Navigable Small World, is the leading ANN algorithm. It builds a multi-layer graph where the top layer has few nodes for coarse navigation and the bottom layer has all nodes for fine-grained search. Think of it as express lanes on a highway.

ML models degrade silently. Data drift means your input distribution has changed. Concept drift means the relationship between features and labels has shifted. Monitor prediction distributions and retrain when drift is detected.

Putting it all together: data sources feed the feature store. The training pipeline reads features and produces models. The serving layer loads models and serves predictions. A/B testing validates improvements. Monitoring closes the feedback loop.

segments.thought_prompt: Your model's accuracy drops 5% on Monday mornings. What could cause this, and how would you investigate?

segments.text: It is probably data drift tied to a weekly pattern, like different user behavior on Mondays. Check your feature distributions by day of week. ML system design is where software engineering meets data science. Master both, and you are invaluable.
